name: Attendance and Early Warning
title: Attendance and Early Warning
answer: Attendance and early warning is the practice of using school data to spot students whose absences are rising or who may be at risk of failing or dropping out, then pairing that flag with a person who follows up. It matters because chronic absence is one of the clearest signs a student is struggling, and a flag only helps when a human acts on it.

sections.body: Chronic absence is one of the clearest warning signs that a student is struggling, so schools watch attendance data for early signals. Messages to parents about their child's absences do reduce chronic absence, but messaging alone is only part of the answer. The strongest approach pairs the data with a person: a system flags students whose absences are rising, and an attendance worker, counselor, or teacher follows up. Early warning systems go further and predict which students are at risk of failing or dropping out. The idea solves the problem of struggling students going unnoticed until it is too late, while keeping the response human rather than mechanical.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a student information system flags students whose absences are rising, and an attendance worker, counselor, or teacher follows up with a call home, a meeting, or a visit. That follow up is how staff learn what is actually happening, such as a student caring for a sick parent, being bullied, or missing the bus. Early warning systems add predictions about which students are at risk of failing or dropping out, and machine learning can improve those predictions. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea. The follow up is the point of the practice, because the person, not the flag, finds the reason behind the absences.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support. It states that messages to parents about their child's absences reduce chronic absence, with effects of 10 to 15 percent in the original trials and smaller effects in newer ones run at scale (Rogers & Feller, 2018; Robinson et al., 2018; Berger et al., 2025). A meta analysis of 13 recent studies of attendance interventions found a small average effect, stronger when carried out within a single school (Li, 2026). On early warning systems, the text cites Soland et al. (2020) for the finding that machine learning can improve predictions but takes expertise to use well, and that results from systems whose reasoning is hidden can be read through staff members' existing biases. It also cites Hlosta et al. (2022), whose interviews with students whose risk predictions were wrong found the errors came from sudden life events such as family changes, health problems, or computer trouble.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A flag is a reason for a conversation, not a judgment about who a student is, and early warning flags should never follow a student as labels. Staff should be trained to see flags this way. Students and families should never be told that a computer has decided a child is at risk. Predictions are also wrong in ways that matter, since sudden life events can cause errors, and hidden reasoning in a system can be read through staff members' existing biases. The decisions that stay with a person are the follow up and the judgment about what a flag means for a particular student.
